newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS - Asian EMU fears hit investment - HK c.banker.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Asian EMU fears hit investment - HK c.banker.

text.p: Asian investors are cutting back on investments in Europe as they are worried by insecurity ahead of European currency union, Joseph Yam, chief executive of the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, said on Thursday.

"We have been reducing our exposure to European investments. We do not know what is going on with European currency union," he told a conference here on Hong Kong's monetary arrangements through 1997.
"Only after the euro is firmly established can we be sure. In the meantime, if we want to manage risk, we have to reduce our exposure to Europe," said Yam.
Yam's comments have opened up another can of worms in the increasingly torrid debate on EMU, scheduled to start in 1999.
There have been fears of late that not enough countries, including Germany, will meet the required entry criteria.
"We are concerned about the uncertainties surrounding EMU and their possible impact on the performance of financial markets in Europe," Yam said.

Yam pointed out that Asian economies are substantial holders of the world's official foreign reserves, with five out of the seven largest foreign reserves holders in the world based in Asia, managing a total of around $600 billion.

"Potential considerations in the management of public funds require the adoption of risk-averse strategies, in this case possibly a reduction of exposure, with implications for the stability of financial markets in Europe, at least before the euro has been firmly established," Yam said.
Yam said that 75 percent of Hong Kong's reserves were held in U.S. dollar related investments, so the maximum European exposure was 25 percent.

In launching a counter-assault on Europe's weakest flank -- possible instability in advance of EMU in 1999 -- Yam turned the tables on European investors sceptical about Hong Kong's ability to remain independent after Hong Kong reverts to Chinese rule at the end of June 1997.
European investors' worries focus on what happens after the handover and they fear China will try to milk Hong Kong of its wealth.
The Basic Law, which outlines China's plans for governing the territory post-1997, says Hong Kong will maintain independent finances, manage its own economic policy and keep free trade.
The message from assembled central and commercial bankers from Hong Kong and mainland China at the conference, organised by Germany's Dresdner Bank, was an upbeat one.

Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said he was watching China and Hong Kong's attempts to bring in a system where both the Hong Kong dollar and the Chinese Renminbi operate side-by-side, but mutually independently.

He said Europe was trying to do something similar, but the other way around, by introducing one currency for several countries. "Our preparations for monetary union are not so far developed as Hong Kong and China's monetary plans," he said.
Chen Yuan, Deputy Governor of the People's Bank of China, said that the Hong Kong dollar would continue to be tied to the U.S. dollar at HK$7.80.
Chen again underlined the "high degree of autonomy" to be enjoyed by Hong Kong after the handover.
Xuebing Wang, Chairman and President of the Bank of China, said that Hong Kong will play an increasingly important role in helping fund the economic development of China beyond 1997.
"Hong Kong is by far the largest direct external investor in the mainland of China," he said.

"In 1996, $15.1 billion FDI (Foreign Direct Investment) has flowed from Hong Kong into the mainland of China, which pushed the total from Hong Kong to China to over $93.7 billion, 57 percent of total FDI into mainland China since 1979," he said.
